svg.aria-label: Diagram: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity now accepts OAuth 2.0 authorization server discovery URLs as well as OIDC ones, for both inbound JWT authorization and outbound OAuth credential providers, in all Regions where AgentCore is available and at no additional cost. The change is one alternation in the discovery URL validation pattern, which must match a well-known path ending in either openid-configuration or oauth-authorization-server, the latter being OAuth 2.0 Authorization Server Metadata as defined by RFC 8414, and the pattern also permits an optional path segment after the well-known component. The authorizer is identity-provider agnostic and works with any OAuth 2.0 compatible identity provider, and on each inbound request it uses the configured discovery URL to fetch the public keys and authorization server endpoint to perform JWT validation, which is what lets AgentCore Identity dynamically accept tokens without explicit onboarding. The validation contract is unchanged. The discovery URL should point to an issuer URL that matches the iss claim in the decoded token. At least one of four fields is required: allowed audiences validated against the aud claim, allowed clients validated against the client_id claim, allowed scopes where at least one scope value in the token must match one configured value, or required custom claims, which match a named claim against a value using EQUALS for a STRING type and CONTAINS or CONTAINS_ANY for a STRING_ARRAY type. If more than one field is used the authorizer verifies them all, so within a field the semantics are any and across fields the semantics are all, meaning each field added narrows access rather than widening it. The same authorizer configuration applies to AgentCore Runtime and AgentCore Gateway. A runtime can support either IAM SigV4 or JWT bearer token inbound auth but not both simultaneously, so switching mode means a new version. When no bearer token is supplied the service returns 401 Unauthorized with a WWW-Authenticate header per RFC 7235, pointing at protected resource metadata so clients can discover which authorization servers protect the agent, though an OAuth client must still be pre-registered to obtain a client_id before using the discovered endpoints. For outbound access the Token Vault binds a cached third-party token using the agent workload identity and the user ID taken from the inbound JWT token, which is the assumption to check when tokens are machine-to-machine.
svg.title: One alternation in a validation pattern, and OIDC stops being required
svg.text: The whole feature is one alternation in a validation pattern.
“You can configure AgentCore with authorization servers that implement OAuth 2.0 without OIDC.”
The discovery URL pattern — two accepted document names, one of them new
^[^\s?#]+/\.well-known/(openid-configuration|oauth-authorization-server)(/[^\s?#]+)?$
openid-configuration — OIDC discovery, accepted before and now.
oauth-authorization-server — “OAuth 2.0 Authorization Server Metadata (RFC 8414)”. This is the change.
WHAT DISCOVERY BUYS
The authorizer fetches “the public keys and
authorization server endpoint” per request.
“… dynamically accept tokens … without
explicit onboarding.” No key upload, no rotation dance.
WHAT IT DOES NOT CHANGE
“The discovery url should point to an issuer url.
This should match the iss claim in the decoded token.”
A trailing slash is a mismatch. Compare the strings
before you debug anything else.
Any within a field. All across fields.
“At least one of the fields is required … If more than one is used, the authorizer will verify them all.”
allowed audiences → aud
allowed clients → client_id
allowed scopes → scope (one token value must match one configured value)
required custom claims → EQUALS | CONTAINS | CONTAINS_ANY, by declared type
ONE INBOUND MODE PER RUNTIME
“either IAM SigV4 or JWT Bearer Token … but not
both simultaneously.” Changing it means a version.
THE 401 TELLS A CLIENT WHERE, NOT WHO
WWW-Authenticate points at protected-resource
metadata — but you still pre-register for a client_id.
Outbound: the Token Vault binds a cached third-party token to “the agent workload identity and user ID (from the
inbound JWT token)” — the assumption to check when your tokens are machine-to-machine and carry no user.
OAuth 2.0 without OIDC proves a grant, not a person. Inbound auth is fine with that; your binding key may not be.
